topics.title: Stoicism in five ideas
topics.dek: A Greek porch, a Roman emperor and a philosophy built for bad days

slides.p: Zeno of Citium began teaching in Athens around 300 BC at the Stoa Poikile, the painted colonnade, which gave the school its name. It ran for five centuries. Its best-known writers were a Roman statesman (Seneca), a freed slave (Epictetus) and an emperor (Marcus Aurelius) who wrote notes to himself in a tent on the Danube.

slides.h: 1. Some things are up to you; most aren't
slides.p: Epictetus opens his handbook with it: our judgments, intentions and efforts are ours; our bodies, reputations, property and other people are not fully. Misery comes from treating the second kind as the first. Put your energy where it has purchase and hold the rest loosely.

slides.h: 2. It's not the event, it's the judgment
slides.p: 'People are disturbed not by things but by the views they take of things.' The traffic jam is a fact; the fury is an opinion added to it. The Stoics practised noticing the gap between the two and choosing what to add. Modern cognitive behavioral therapy was built on exactly this idea.

slides.h: 3. Virtue is the only real good
slides.p: Wisdom, justice, courage and self-control are good in themselves; health, wealth and reputation are 'preferred indifferents', worth pursuing but not worth selling your character for. The point isn't austerity. Seneca was rich. The point is that a good life can't be taken from you by bad luck.

Premeditatio malorum: each morning, picture the day's likely setbacks, the rude colleague, the delay, the loss, so they arrive expected rather than as insults. Seneca went further and recommended occasional days of plain food and rough clothes, to learn that the thing you fear is survivable.

items: Morning: what could go wrong today?
Meet it when it comes, already prepared
Evening: review what you did and would change

slides.p: Memento mori wasn't morbid; it was a lens. Marcus reminds himself that everyone he envies and everyone who annoys him will be dust, and so will he, so he had better do the day's work with care and not waste it on resentment. Mortality is the deadline that makes priorities obvious.

v.q: You could leave life right now. Let that determine what you do and say and think.

slides.p: Not suppressing emotion: the Stoics wanted fewer destructive passions, not numbness, and cared intensely about justice and other people. Not passivity: Marcus ran an empire and fought wars. Not 'stoic' in the modern stiff-upper-lip sense. It's a training programme for attention and judgment.

items: Choosing your judgments, acting on duty, holding results loosely

slides.p: Each morning, name one thing in your control and one that isn't. Each evening, three lines: what went well, what didn't, what you'd do differently. When something stings, say 'this is an impression' and wait a beat. That is the whole practice, and it is older than the Roman Empire.

quiz.q: The dichotomy of control says to focus effort on…
a: Your own judgments, choices and efforts
quiz.why: Those are the things that are fully up to you. Outcomes and others' views are influenced, never controlled.

quiz.q: 'People are disturbed not by things but by the views they take of things' is the root of…
quiz.why: CBT's founders credited the Stoics directly for the idea that the judgment, not the event, drives the emotion.

quiz.q: Marcus Aurelius wrote the Meditations as…
quiz.why: They were never meant for publication, which is why they read like someone talking himself through hard days.

take: Separate what's up to you from what isn't; spend yourself on the first.
The judgment, not the event, makes the emotion; there's a gap, and you can use it.
Rehearse setbacks, remember mortality, review the day: a practice, not a mood.

topics.title: How to look at a painting
topics.dek: Six questions that turn a glance into seeing

slides.h: Give it more than eight seconds
slides.p: Museum visitors spend a median of about 15 to 30 seconds in front of a work, much of it reading the label. The method on these cards takes three or four minutes and works on anything from a Vermeer to your kid's drawing. Look first; read the label last.

slides.h: 1. Where does your eye go first, and then?
slides.p: Painters steer the eye: with the brightest spot, the sharpest contrast, a face, a pointing hand, lines that lead. Notice your first landing and the path after it. That route is usually the story the painter wants told in order.

Composition is the skeleton. Look for the big shapes: a triangle (stable, classical), a diagonal (energy), a horizontal band (calm), a frame within the frame. Where is the horizon? Is the subject centered or pushed to an edge, and what does the empty space do?

slides.h: 3. Where is the light coming from?
slides.p: Find the shadows and you find the light source. Single hard light from the side (Caravaggio, Rembrandt) is drama; soft light from a window (Vermeer) is intimacy; flat, even light (much modern painting) refuses to tell you what to feel. Light is the painter's mood lighting.

Is the palette warm or cool, saturated or muted, and is there one color that breaks the rule? Complementary pairs (red against green, orange against blue) make each other vibrate; a single warm note in a cool picture is often the point. Squint and the color scheme reveals itself.

Get close. Thick, visible strokes (impasto) say speed and feeling; glassy invisible surfaces say patience and control. Is it oil, which blends and glows; tempera, which is crisp; watercolor, which stains and can't be undone; or fresco, painted into wet plaster? The hand is in the surface.

items: into wet plaster, by the day

slides.h: 6. What was it for, and who paid?
slides.p: Now read the label. An altarpiece was made to be seen by candlelight from below; a portrait was flattery with a bill attached; a history painting was propaganda for a salon; an Impressionist canvas was made to be sold to a new middle class. Purpose explains size, subject and style.

slides.h: Then say one true thing about it
slides.p: Out loud or in a notebook: 'The light comes from the left and the only warm color is her sleeve.' Not whether it's good, not what it means, just one thing you saw. Do that with ten paintings and you'll start seeing the eleventh before the label can tell you what to think.

items: Purpose: who paid, read the label

quiz.q: The fastest way to find a painting's light source is to…
quiz.why: Shadows point away from the light. Hard single shadows mean one dramatic source; soft ones mean diffuse light.

quiz.q: A composition built on strong diagonals usually feels…
quiz.why: Horizontals and triangles read as stable; diagonals and cropped edges read as movement.

quiz.q: Complementary colors placed side by side…
a: Make each other look more intense
quiz.why: Red beside green, orange beside blue: each heightens the other, which painters use to make a small note sing.

take: Look before you read; follow where your eye is led.
Composition, light, color, surface: the four things to find in any picture.
Finish with one true sentence about what you saw.

topics.title: Classical music: the eras and what to hear
topics.dek: Six periods in six cards, with one piece to start each

slides.h: 'Classical' is six centuries, not one style
slides.p: The label covers Western art music from medieval chant to living composers. The useful map is six eras, each with a sound you can learn to recognise in a few listens. Dates overlap; styles arrived in different places at different times. Start anywhere.

Gregorian chant is a single melodic line, unaccompanied, for worship. From about 1100 composers stacked independent voices (polyphony), and by the Renaissance (Josquin, Palestrina, Tallis) four to forty voices wove together in church and in secular madrigals. Instruments were mostly for dancing.

Opera is invented (Monteverdi, 1607). Music gets a driving bass line (basso continuo), terraced loud-and-soft dynamics, and endless ornament. Bach builds fugues, Vivaldi writes 500 concertos, Handel writes Messiah in 24 days. The harpsichord's pluck is the era's signature sound.

Reaction against Baroque density: clear melodies over simple accompaniment, balanced phrases, and sonata form (a theme stated, developed, returned) as the engine of symphonies, string quartets and sonatas. Haydn invents much of it, Mozart perfects it, Beethoven breaks it open. The piano replaces the harpsichord.

Beethoven's late works point the way: music as the composer's inner life. Orchestras double in size, symphonies run an hour, harmony stretches toward breaking (Wagner's Tristan chord, 1865). Chopin writes for the piano alone; Verdi and Wagner build opera into national theatre; Tchaikovsky, Brahms and Dvořák fill concert halls.

Debussy dissolves the key; Stravinsky's Rite of Spring causes a riot in 1913 with its pounding rhythms; Schoenberg abandons tonality for the twelve-tone row; Bartók folds in folk music; Shostakovich writes under Stalin; after 1945 minimalists (Reich, Glass) build hypnotic repetition, and film scores carry the orchestra to all.

items: Debussy, Prélude à l'après-midi d'un faune

slides.h: What to listen for in any piece
slides.p: Find the pulse and whether it's in twos or threes. Find the tune and notice when it comes back, and changed how. Notice which instrument has it and who's accompanying. Listen for the loudest moment and ask how long the composer made you wait for it. That's most of music appreciation.

items: Tension and release: where's the peak?

slides.p: One per era, each under about fifteen minutes or with a famous movement: Hildegard's O virtus Sapientiae; Tallis's Spem in alium; Bach's Brandenburg Concerto No. 3; Mozart's Symphony No. 40, first movement; Dvořák's Symphony No. 9, Largo; Reich's Music for 18 Musicians, opening. Then follow whatever you liked.

quiz.q: The harpsichord's plucked sound is the signature of which era?
quiz.why: Bach, Handel and Vivaldi wrote for it; the piano, which can play soft and loud, took over in the Classical era.

quiz.q: Sonata form, the engine of Classical-era symphonies, is…
a: A piece for solo piano only
quiz.why: Exposition, development, recapitulation. Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven built symphonies, quartets and sonatas on it.

quiz.q: Which premiere famously caused a riot in Paris in 1913?
quiz.why: Its pounding rhythms and dissonance, plus Nijinsky's choreography, split the audience into shouting factions.

take: Six eras: chant and polyphony, Baroque ornament, Classical form, Romantic feeling, Modern questions.
Listen for pulse, tune, who has it, and where the peak is.
One piece per era, then follow your ear.
src: BBC: A brief history of classical music

topics.title: Jazz in eight cards
topics.dek: From New Orleans to bebop to now: the styles, the names, the records

slides.p: Jazz grew out of ragtime, blues, marching bands and the Caribbean rhythms of a port city, in the Black neighbourhoods of New Orleans. Early bands improvised together over simple chords: trumpet on the tune, clarinet weaving above, trombone below, a rhythm section driving. Buddy Bolden is the legend; no recording of him survives.

Armstrong's Hot Five and Hot Seven records (1925–28) turned jazz from group improvisation into a soloist's art: swinging rhythm, dazzling trumpet lines, and scat singing. 'West End Blues' (1928) is the one to hear. Nearly every jazz musician since has been answering him.

v.q: If you have to ask what jazz is, you'll never know.

slides.h: Swing: the 1930s dance music of America
slides.p: Big bands of 15 or so players with written arrangements and room for soloists: Duke Ellington (the composer), Count Basie (the rhythm), Benny Goodman (the crossover), Ella Fitzgerald and Billie Holiday (the voices). For a decade jazz was pop music, and Goodman's 1938 Carnegie Hall concert made it respectable.

items: Goodman's Palomar date: swing era begins

slides.p: In Harlem after-hours clubs in the early 1940s, Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Thelonious Monk and Bud Powell built a virtuoso music in small groups: fast tempos, complex chords, long improvised lines. It wasn't for dancing. Parker's 'Ko-Ko' (1945) announced it; Monk's tunes are still the repertoire's hardest puzzles.

Miles Davis's Kind of Blue, built on modes instead of chord changes, became the best-selling jazz record ever. Dave Brubeck's Time Out put 5/4 on the radio with 'Take Five'. Ornette Coleman's The Shape of Jazz to Come threw out the chords altogether. Charles Mingus's Mingus Ah Um looked back to gospel and forward to protest.

items: Ornette Coleman, The Shape of Jazz to Come (free)

slides.p: John Coltrane went from the hardest chord changes ever written ('Giant Steps') to modal hymns (A Love Supreme, 1965) to free improvisation in five years. His quartet with McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison and Elvin Jones set the template for intensity. He died at 40 in 1967; a church in San Francisco is named for him.

Miles plugged in: Bitches Brew (1970) mixed jazz improvisation with rock and funk, and his sidemen founded Weather Report, Return to Forever and the Headhunters. The music also went back to the tradition (Wynton Marsalis, 1980s), into hip-hop (A Tribe Called Quest, Robert Glasper, Kendrick Lamar) and around the world.

Find the tune (the 'head'), played at the start. Then each soloist improvises over the same chords for a chorus or several, trading the spotlight; the band comments behind them. The head returns at the end. Count the choruses, hear who's quoting whom, and notice the drummer's conversation with the soloist. That's the form.

a: Turning jazz into a soloist's art with swing and scat
quiz.why: The Hot Five and Hot Seven records (1925–28) made the improvising soloist the center of the music.

quiz.q: Bebop differed from swing in that it was…
a: Faster, harmonically complex, played in small groups for listening
quiz.why: Parker, Gillespie and Monk built a musicians' music in Harlem clubs in the early 1940s.

quiz.q: Kind of Blue (1959) was built on…
a: Modes, with few chords, leaving space to improvise
quiz.why: Modal jazz gave soloists scales rather than dense changes. It's the best-selling jazz album ever made.

take: New Orleans → Armstrong's soloist → swing → bebop → 1959's modal and free turns → fusion → now.
The form: head, solos over the same chords, head out.
Start with West End Blues, Kind of Blue and A Love Supreme.

topics.title: Eight building styles you can name on sight
topics.dek: From Greek columns to glass boxes: what to look for and when it was built

slides.p: Greek temples (c. 600–100 BC) and Roman buildings after them use columns in three orders: Doric (plain capital, no base), Ionic (scroll capital), Corinthian (acanthus leaves). Pediments, symmetry and proportion. The Romans added the arch, the dome and concrete. Banks and courthouses still borrow the look.

Romanesque churches (c. 1000–1150) are heavy: round arches, thick walls, small windows, like fortresses. Gothic (c. 1140–1500) solved the weight problem with pointed arches and flying buttresses that carry the roof's thrust outside, so walls could become glass: Chartres, Notre-Dame, Cologne, the soaring rib vault.

Renaissance (15th–16th c.) revived Roman order: symmetry, columns, round arches, domes, proportion by number (Brunelleschi, Palladio, whose villas became the model for every columned house in Virginia). Baroque (17th c.) took the same vocabulary and made it move: curves, drama, gold, oval plans, Bernini's colonnade, Versailles.

From about 1750, archaeology and the Enlightenment brought back strict Greek and Roman forms: the U.S. Capitol, the Panthéon in Paris, the British Museum. The 19th century then revived everything in turn: Gothic for churches and parliaments (Westminster), Romanesque for libraries, Renaissance for banks. Style became a choice.

Art Nouveau (1890–1910) used iron and glass for plant-like curves: Paris Métro entrances, Gaudí's Barcelona, Horta's Brussels. Art Deco (1920s–30s) went the other way: streamlined, geometric, zigzags and sunbursts, chrome and black glass, the Chrysler Building and Miami Beach hotels. Both are easy to spot and date.

The Bauhaus (1919) and Le Corbusier stripped ornament away: flat roofs, white walls, ribbon windows, open plans, steel and glass, the building as a 'machine for living in'. After 1945 the glass-and-steel tower (Mies's Seagram Building, 1958) became the world's office building. Brutalism poured the same ideas in raw concrete.

items: Lever House: the glass curtain wall

slides.p: By the 1970s modernism's boxes felt cold. Postmodernism (Venturi, Graves, Philip Johnson's AT&T Building with its broken pediment, 1984) brought back color, ornament and jokes. Since the 1990s computers made curves cheap: Gehry's Bilbao (1997), Hadid's swoops, and a green turn toward timber, insulation and reuse.

slides.h: How to date a building in ten seconds
slides.p: Look at the windows and the roofline. Small windows and round arches: Romanesque or its revival. Pointed arches: Gothic or revival. Columns and a pediment: classical, in some century. Zigzags: Deco. Ribbon windows and no ornament: modernist. A curtain of glass: post-1950. A shape you couldn't draw with a ruler: post-1990.

quiz.q: Flying buttresses allowed Gothic cathedrals to have…
a: Huge windows, because the roof's thrust was carried outside the wall
quiz.why: With the load moved to external supports, walls could dissolve into stained glass.

quiz.q: Zigzags, sunbursts and chrome on a 1930 skyscraper point to…
quiz.why: Deco is the streamlined geometry of the 1920s and 30s; Nouveau is the plant-like curves two decades earlier.

quiz.q: 'Form follows function' and ribbon windows belong to…
quiz.why: The Bauhaus and Le Corbusier stripped ornament to express structure and use.

take: Columns and pediments: classical. Pointed arches and buttresses: Gothic. Curves of plants: Nouveau. Zigzags: Deco.
No ornament, ribbon windows, glass: modern. Shapes a ruler can't draw: after 1990.
Windows and roofline date a building fastest.
